crossed.

  • At least one NCD relay board paired with the gateway.

  • data:read — reads telemetry from the platform database (read-only).
  • telemetry:subscribe — receives live sensor frames.
  • relay:command — sends relay commands through the platform.

versions.readme_html:
Filter Monitor

Air filter health from differential pressure: how clogged each HVAC or industrial filter is, how much life is left in it, and when it needs changing.

What it does

  • A card per filter showing used life as a percentage, a colour-coded meter

between the filter's clean and replacement pressures, the live pressure drop across the element, and a plain-language verdict.

  • Knows the difference between a clean filter and a stopped fan. Pressure

drop rises with air speed as well as with dust, so a reading taken while the fan is off says nothing about how dirty the element is — and read naively it looks like a clean filter. Each filter has an airflow floor; readings below it are left out of scoring, the filter is marked idle, and it holds the last verdict measured while air was moving.

  • Learns each filter's clean pressure from its own first hours of running

data, rather than trusting a datasheet figure that assumes an airflow your unit may not run at. An operator who knows the real number can type it in.

  • Pressure trend over 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days, with the clean and

replacement thresholds drawn in and the spread behind the average, so you can see how fast an element is loading and judge when it will need changing.

  • Add-filter wizard that polls the sensor live while you are standing at the

unit, so you can confirm the tubes are on the right way round before saving — and offers a one-click fix if they are reversed. Both thresholds can be captured from the sensor itself, which cancels out its resting offset.

  • Tells you when a sensor goes quiet. A filter whose sensor has missed three

reports keeps its last verdict but stops showing it in a confident colour, and says how long it has been silent.

  • Alerts by email when a filter first reaches its replacement pressure.
  • Works with other apps and AI assistants: publishes each filter's status on

the gateway's app bus, so "filter needs replacing" can be wired to an email or a beacon on the Automations page; offers a Mark replaced action other apps can trigger; and lets an AI assistant connected to the gateway read filter health and pressure history.

Supported sensors

| Type | Sensor | Firmware | |---|---|---| | 21 | Differential Bidirectional Pressure Sensor | 15 or newer | | 20 | Precision Pressure & Temperature (pA) | 6 or newer | | 131 | Wireless Differential Pressure Sensor Gen4 | any |

One tube goes upstream of the filter and one downstream, so the sensor reads the pressure drop across the element directly.

The firmware floors are where each sensor starts reporting a pressure with its unit attached. Below them the only pressure in the frame is a raw number whose unit depends on the chip fitted and is not discoverable, so the app declines the sensor rather than guessing — a wrong unit would put a wrong percentage in front of a maintenance decision. Filter Monitor also warns when a filter's replacement pressure is beyond what its sensor can measure.

Requirements

  • Atrium platform 2.6.0 or newer.
  • One of the supported sensors per filter, paired with the gateway and plumbed

across the element.

Configuration

Add each filter through the wizard: name and location, filter type, the clean and replacement pressures, then the sensor. Settings covers the display unit (inches of water or Pascals), how far back readings are considered, how long a new filter learns its clean baseline, and how many readings a verdict is smoothed over.

Marking a filter replaced resets its life, timestamps the change in its service history, and starts re-learning the clean baseline if it was learning one.

Licensing

Filter Monitor is free. No license is needed to install or use it.

# Changelog

## 1.0.0

- **First App Center release.** No functional change from 0.7.1.
- Requires Atrium 2.6.0. Reads the Differential Bidirectional Pressure Sensor
  (type 21, firmware 15+), the Precision Pressure & Temperature pA sensor
  (type 20, firmware 6+) and the Wireless Differential Pressure Sensor Gen4
  (type 131). Older type 21 firmware is declined rather than guessed at — only
  firmware 15 reports a unit-typed pressure.

## 0.7.1

Fixes from the hardware test on gateway AFE6, where the app was run against a
bench duct rig with a type 21 sensor and a Dwyer Magnehelic teed across the same
ports.

- **Fixed: a filter went blank for about half an hour after every shutdown.**
  The rig was switched off overnight; in the morning, with the fan running
  again, every filter read "No data — not enough running readings yet". The
  evaluation window is six hours, so an overnight stop empties it, and scoring
  started again from zero. Most air handlers stop nightly or at weekends, so
  this would have happened on every site, every morning. The element does not
  load while the fan is off, so the last verdict is still the best information:
  it is now held and marked **re-checking** until fresh readings can confirm it.

- **Fixed: the pressure trend charted readings from before the filter existed.**
  Commissioning — bench-testing a sensor, dipping it in a water column — puts
  pressures through the chart that a filter never sees; 173 in. w.c. was
  recorded, which squashed the clean and replacement lines onto each other and
  made the chart useless. The trend now starts no earlier than the filter was
  created, and the y-axis is scaled to the element in front of you rather than
  to every value ever recorded. Where a filter has had more than one element, a
  button switches between all of them and the current one.

- **Fixed: a filter at its replacement pressure could still read "Due soon".**
  The card showed "1.45, replace at 1.45" and 99.9% used, because the stored
  values differed by less than the displayed unit resolves. The verdict is now
  decided at the precision shown, and a percentage just below the threshold
  shows one decimal rather than rounding to a flat "100%".

- **Thresholds can be captured from the sensor.** Every pressure sensor rests at
  some offset — the one on the rig sat at +0.04 in. w.c. — so a clean pressure
  typed from a reference gauge made a clean filter read 5.6% used. Taking both
  numbers from the same sensor that does the scoring cancels the offset exactly.
  The wizard's sensor step now has **Clean** and **Replace at** buttons that
  capture the live reading, and the thresholds step says why this is worth doing.

- **The live pressure is always shown.** It used to be replaced by an em dash
  until a filter could be scored, which is exactly when an installer is trying
  to confirm the tubes are on. The card now leads with the live value and says
  what it is waiting for, with a count.

- **The sensor's measuring range is now known for the AMS5812.** No full scale
  was derived for that chip, so the range check quietly skipped every type 21
  sensor: a part fitted with the wrong range read 3x low, then 67x high, with no
  warning. The suffixes are tenths of a psi.

- **"Last reading" named two different things** — a pressure and a time. The
  time is now **Last heard**, matching the rest of Atrium.

- **The trend has 1 h and 6 h ranges.** At 24 h the buckets are six minutes
  wide, so a bench test drew one or two points.

- Life used is clamped on the chart; a single bad sample was able to report
  five-figure percentages.

- The README documents the bench-testing traps: set **Median over** to 1 when
  stepping a rig through loading states by hand, and take thresholds from the
  NCD sensor rather than a reference gauge.

## 0.7.0

- **Two more sensors are supported.** Alongside the Differential Bidirectional
  Pressure Sensor (type 21, firmware 15+), the app now drives the **Wireless
  Differential Pressure Sensor Gen4** (type 131, any firmware) and the
  **Precision Pressure & Temperature (pA)** sensor (type 20, firmware 6+). All
  three report a differential pressure with its unit attached, which is what lets
  one app read them identically; each has its own firmware floor and sensors
  below it are listed with the reason rather than hidden.

- **The Gen4's measuring range is read from its telemetry.** It reports its range
  on every data frame rather than in a configuration check-in, so the app knows
  which Honeywell ADP part is fitted — and therefore whether a filter's
  replacement pressure is within what the sensor can measure — as soon as the
  sensor reports, without any pairing step.

- **The pressure trend opens as a window** over the dashboard, from a **View
  trend** button. The buttons on each card — View trend, Edit, Mark replaced,
  Remove — are now always visible, and clicking the card itself no longer does
  anything, so nothing is hidden behind a click you had to guess at.

- **Sensor temperature is shown on the trend window.** All three sensors report
  it. It is context only and plays no part in the filter calculation, which its
  tooltip says.

- A sensor range warning no longer reappears for a newly created filter when the
  same sensor has already shown readings beyond the range it claims.

- **The controls and severity counts stay on screen while the list scrolls**, so
  the counts remain usable as filters however many filters there are. An **All**
  count sits at the front of the row as an explicit way back to the full list.

- **A full-screen button** widens the dashboard to use the whole frame. Where the
  browser permits it the page also goes genuinely full screen; where it does not
  — which includes the gateway's own sandboxed frame — the widened layout still
  applies, so the button always does something.

- **Warnings moved off the cards into a notice button.** Cards were growing to
  different heights depending on whether anything was wrong; an amber warning
  icon now appears beside the other actions, and opens a window carrying the
  filter's name, its sensor address and the full text.

- **Fixed: adding a filter opened its pressure trend by itself.** The trend now
  opens only from View trend.

- The pressure trend window shows the sensor's address under the filter name.

## 0.6.0

- **Fixed: a filter could stay on "Replace now" after being marked replaced.**
  Readings taken before the element went in were still being scored, so the old
  filter's high pressures out-voted the new one's for hours. Only readings from
  the current element are scored now. The same fix means a filter created today
  ignores whatever the sensor reported while it was being commissioned.

- **"In service since" can be edited**, with a "Start fresh now" button beside
  it. This is how to discard test or commissioning data: nothing recorded before
  that moment is ever scored. The app does not store telemetry of its own — the
  readings belong to the gateway and are kept under its own retention settings —
  so moving this date is the way to draw a line under old data rather than
  deleting anything.

- **The pressure trend marks where the element was replaced**, so a step down in
  the line explains itself.

- **Fixed: marking a filter replaced raised two false warnings** — that the
  sensor had stopped reporting, and that the replacement pressure was outside the
  sensor's range. Both facts belong to the sensor rather than to the filter
  element, and both were being discarded along with the old verdict. A
  freshly replaced filter now simply says it is waiting for its first reading.

- **"Installed" moved to the filter card**, beside "last reading", and shows how
  long the current element has been in service.

- **The smoothed pressure is labelled correctly.** It was shown as "avg of last
  5" but has always been the median — the middle reading, which is what stops one
  odd value moving a maintenance decision. It now says so, and the number of
  readings it spans is adjustable from the toolbar.

- **Differential pressure leads with the value the percentage uses**, with the
  latest reading beneath it.

- **The pressure trend marks every element change in view**, not only the most
  recent, and service history scrolls after three entries instead of growing the
  panel.

- **"% of filter life used" explains itself** on hover — what it measures, what
  it is calculated from, and when it updates.

## 0.5.0

- **A Data Timeout Limit can now be set per filter**, in the setup wizard and
  when editing: if no data arrives within it, the filter is flagged as having
  stopped reporting. Left empty it follows the sensor's own
  reporting interval — three missed reports, so a sensor reporting every 10
  minutes is flagged after 30 — which is the right behaviour for almost everyone
  and adapts automatically if the transmission rate is changed. Set it yourself
  when the reporting interval recorded against the sensor is out of date, or when
  a longer grace period suits the site.

- **Tooltips now open wherever there is room** — below the icon normally, beside
  it when the window is short. They previously always opened downward and could
  run off the bottom of a small window.

- **Removed "checked" from the cards and the pressure trend.** "Last reading" is
  the field that matters; when the app last recalculated was noise.

- **The pressure trend panel now shows only what it adds** — the thresholds, the
  baseline, the pressure chip, the install date and how much data backs the
  chart. Everything it used to repeat is on the card behind it.

- **The sensor's address is on the filter card**, under the location, rather than
  buried in the trend panel — it identifies the filter rather than explaining the
  chart. The Data Timeout Limit sits under "last reading", next to the number it
  governs.

## 0.4.0

- **"Last reading" is now on every filter card**, next to "checked". They are
  different facts: the app keeps recalculating on schedule even when a sensor has
  gone silent, so "checked 5m ago" said nothing about whether data was still
  arriving. A filter that has missed three expected reports is now marked stale,
  its card drops the confident colour, and it says how long it has been quiet and
  what to check.

- **Each card carries its status colour down its left edge**, so a wall of
  filters can be read at a glance without opening anything.

- **Differential pressure shows both numbers**: the live reading, and underneath
  it the average the percentage was actually calculated from.

- **Airflow says it describes the last reading**, not this instant, and its
  tooltip lists what Running, Idle and Unknown each mean.

- **The setup wizard warns when a filter's pressures sit outside the sensor's
  stated measuring range** — as a warning, not a block. The range comes from
  configuration the sensor reported at a past check-in and is occasionally out of
  date, so refusing to continue on its word would stop a legitimate setup. If the
  sensor has actually reported beyond its claimed range, the claim is treated as
  disproved and nothing is said.

- **Fixed a range warning that came back overnight.** Whether a sensor has ever
  exceeded its stated range is now remembered rather than being re-derived from
  the last few hours, so the evidence no longer expires with the readings that
  provided it.

- The inter-app bus event now carries `stale` and `last_reading_ts`, so an
  operator can wire "this filter's sensor went quiet" to an alert.

## 0.3.0

- **"Airflow" now describes the present.** It was answering "did anything in the
  last six hours move air?", so a filter kept reporting Running for hours after
  its fan stopped. It is now decided by the sensor's latest reading.

- **The differential pressure shown is the live reading.** It was the average
  across the whole evaluation window, which meant it could not reflect what the
  sensor had just reported — with fifty readings in the window, a real change had
  to out-number all of them before anything moved on screen.

- **The percentage now follows recent readings.** It is taken from the middle of
  the last five readings taken while air was moving, rather than from the whole
  window. Still smoothed enough that one spike cannot change a verdict, but it
  now responds within a few reports instead of hours. The filter's detail panel
  shows both numbers — the live reading and the value the percentage came from —
  each with an explanation.

- **The pressure trend opens on the last 24 hours** instead of 7 days, and now
  has a legend: what the orange line is, what the shaded band around it means,
  and which dashed line is "clean" and which is "replace at".

- A sensor range warning no longer appears and disappears as the fan stops and
  starts; whether the sensor has ever read beyond its stated range is judged
  across the window rather than from the instantaneous value.

## 0.2.0

- **Requires sensor firmware 15 or newer.** Only firmware 15 reports a
  differential pressure with its unit attached. On older firmware the raw
  pressure value's unit depends on which pressure chip is fitted and cannot be
  read from the data, so the app would have had to guess — and a wrong guess puts
  a wrong percentage in front of a maintenance decision. Sensors that can't be
  used now appear in the list with the reason instead of quietly going missing.

- **The sensor's pressure chip and measuring range are read automatically**, from
  what the sensor reports at each check-in, and shown when picking a sensor and
  on the filter's detail. Where the range is in known units the app also warns if
  a filter's replacement pressure sits beyond what the sensor can physically
  measure.

- **Readings now appear as they arrive.** Previously a new reading could sit for
  up to five minutes before the dashboard reflected it, including the "checked"
  time. The verdict is now recomputed as soon as the sensor reports.

- **Filters can be edited.** Name, location, size, thresholds and alert address,
  without removing and re-adding.

- **Explanations where the decisions are made.** The rating standards (MERV,
  ISO 16890, EN 779, HEPA/ULPA) are described in the wizard, and every figure on
  the pressure trend has a short note on what it means.

- Smaller things: the whole filter card opens its trend, not just the header; the
  trend closes with a button, a click outside or Escape; the wizard closes the
  same way; the trend's time axis shows minutes; and sensors are identified by
  the last four bytes of their address rather than the full one, since the
  leading bytes are identical across every radio on a site.

## 0.1.0

First release.

- **Monitor air filters by differential pressure.** Link an NCD Differential
  Bidirectional Pressure Sensor (type 21) across a filter and the app reports how
  much of the element's usable life has been consumed, colour-coded from clean
  through to replace-now.

- **Readings are only scored while air is actually moving.** Pressure drop
  depends on airflow as well as on how dirty a filter is, so a reading taken with
  the fan off would otherwise look like a brand-new filter. Each filter has an
  airflow threshold; below it the app reports the system as idle and holds the
  last severity it measured under airflow instead of showing a falsely clean
  result.

- **Clean baselines are measured, not assumed.** By default a new filter learns
  its own clean pressure from its first hours of running airflow, which is more
  accurate than a datasheet figure that assumes a design airflow your unit may
  not run at. If you know the real number you can enter it instead.

- **Guided setup with a live plumbing check.** The add-filter wizard covers
  naming, filter class (MERV, ISO 16890, EN 779 and HEPA presets with typical
  clean and replacement pressures), thresholds and sensor linking. The sensor
  step shows the live reading as you connect the tubes, and because the sensor is
  bidirectional it detects a reversed pair and offers to correct it with one
  click — before the filter is saved.

- **Email when a filter is due.** One message per filter the first time it
  reaches its replacement pressure, via the gateway's configured SMTP server.

- **Works with automations and with an AI assistant.** Publishes each filter's
  current state to the inter-app bus, so you can wire "filter needs replacing" to
  an email, a beacon or anything else on the Automations page. Provides a "mark
  as replaced" action, and exposes filter health and pressure trends to an
  assistant connected over MCP, answered against the thresholds you configured
  rather than a generic rule.

Requires platform 2.6.0.

versions.readme_html:
AssetPulse

Predictive maintenance for rotating equipment: set up assets, monitor vibration, and get plain-language health insights.

What it does

  • Organize your plant into assets (motors, pumps, fans, gearboxes) and pair

each with a vibration sensor.

  • Continuously monitors vibration and surfaces developing faults before they

cause unplanned downtime.

  • Turns the analysis into plain-language health insights so you don't need a

vibration analyst to act on the data.

  • Waveform history and export — step through past captures with ‹ Older /

Newer › to compare them directly, and download any capture as a .zip containing the raw time-domain samples as CSV plus a JSON sidecar with the asset, drivetrain, sensor and bearing context needed to analyse it elsewhere.

  • Takes part in gateway automations — publishes asset health and threshold

crossings that other apps can react to, and offers actions they can trigger: capture a waveform, acknowledge alerts, send a health email, or set an alarm threshold.

  • Answers questions from an AI assistant connected to the gateway — the

asset roster, how each machine is built, and what its alarm limits are.

  • Optionally publishes to MQTT — stream summary telemetry, waveform captures,

AI reports, and alerts to your own broker on operator-defined topics.

Requirements

  • Atrium platform 2.4.0 or newer.
  • An EG5120 gateway, or Atrium running in a container. The vibration

analysis is CPU-intensive, so AssetPulse is not supported on the EG5100.

  • One or more NCD vibration sensors paired with the gateway.

Two features need a newer platform and are simply not offered on an older one — AssetPulse installs and runs either way:

  • AI-agent access (the reads below) needs platform 2.6.0.
  • Routing AI reports through an AI gateway needs a platform that supports it.

Licensing

AssetPulse is free. No license is needed to install or use it.

Configuration

  • AI & Reports (optional) — generate plain-language reports from an AI

provider. Start by choosing the Connection: Direct to AI provider, or Through an AI proxy (AI gateway) for sites whose policy is that all AI traffic goes through an approved gateway. A proxy asks for its base URL, which API it presents (OpenAI Responses, OpenAI Chat Completions, or Anthropic Messages), the model route your proxy administrator gave you, and the proxy's own token — not the model vendor's, since the proxy holds that credential. Any extra headers live under Advanced. Test validates the configuration before you save.

Whichever connection you choose, the key is encrypted on the gateway and never displayed again, outbound calls follow the gateway's proxy settings, and what is sent is structured evidence only — never raw waveforms.

  • Notifications (optional) — email maintenance staff on severity increases;

requires SMTP configured on the gateway.

  • MQTT (optional) — enable MQTT publishing and set a topic template per data

stream (Summary, Waveform, AI Reports, Alerts). Topics support ::Token:: replacement (asset name, gateway id, sensor id, etc.); leave a topic blank to disable that stream. The gateway's broker connection is configured in the platform's Settings → MQTT Client, where the operator must also grant AssetPulse permission to publish.

  • Automations — Settings → Automations lists everything AssetPulse

offers the gateway bus, plus each asset's currently published health. You wire those to other apps on the platform's Automations page.

  • AI-agent access (optional, platform 2.6.0+) — AssetPulse's reads are

reachable only by an API token or connected app you grant the App data (apps:data) scope. Nothing is exposed until you grant it.

Permissions

  • data:read — reads telemetry from the platform database (read-only).
  • telemetry:subscribe — receives live sensor frames for alert evaluation.
  • radio:fft — requests and analyzes raw vibration waveforms.
  • notify:email — sends fault/alert emails via the gateway mailer.
  • net:external — reaches the configured AI provider or AI gateway for reports.
  • secrets — stores the AI provider or proxy key encrypted at rest.
  • mqtt:client — publishes on the gateway's shared MQTT client (the operator

must also grant AssetPulse in Settings → MQTT Client).

  • events:publish — announces asset health and threshold state on the gateway's

inter-app bus.

  • actions:provide — lets an automation trigger a waveform capture, an alert

acknowledgement, a health email, or a threshold change.

  • mcp:tools — opts AssetPulse into AI-agent access, so the reads listed above

can be called by an assistant you have granted the App data scope.

# Changelog

## 1.9.11

- **Installs on a container deployment.** AssetPulse can now be installed on
  Atrium running in a container, as well as on the EG5120. It remains
  unavailable on the EG5100.
- **AssetPulse is free.** No license is needed to install or use it; this has
  been true since 1.8.0 and is the first App Center release to reflect it.
- Severity's machine-off floor is now learned from line velocity, the same
  measure severity is scored on, so the gap between line and ISO overall
  velocity (mostly the sensor's own electronics) is no longer read as a fault.

## 1.9.10

- **Captures can be held out of a monitoring point's machine-off reference.** The
  reference is what sub-synchronous findings are judged against, so anything
  wrong in it suppresses real findings as "ambient" — the opposite of what it is
  for. The engine already refuses captures it can recognise as unsuitable (a
  machine that was actually running, or one whose sensor had filtering
  disabled), but some it cannot: a capture taken with the sensor unmounted looks
  exactly like a normal quiet one. There is now an exclusion list for those.
- Unusually loud captures are dropped from the reference automatically, so a
  passing forklift does not raise the floor for every later reading.
- Requires Atrium 2.6.12.

## 1.9.9

- **The ISO velocity now says how much of it is the machine.** Double
  integration weights low frequencies heavily, so site vibration below about
  25 Hz can dominate the figure on a quiet machine — on the bench rig the same
  band reads 1.0-1.9 mm/s with the motor stopped. Each assessment now reports
  the velocity split into shaft-synchronous and non-synchronous, and where the
  point has learned a machine-off floor, the ISO term is flagged when the
  running reading does not stand clear of it. Nothing is subtracted: the
  reading is what it is, and the zone is unchanged. What changes is that a
  reading dominated by the site is no longer presented as machine condition.
- The report writer is told what the split means, so it stops reading a zone as
  machine condition when most of the energy is not the machine.
- Requires Atrium 2.6.11.

## 1.9.8

- **The machine-off reference now has to span time.** It was a median over the
  most recent stopped captures, which on a shop floor describes whichever few
  minutes those captures happened to cover. Ambient here moved by nearly 2x
  within two hours, and low-frequency content that dominated one morning was
  gone by that evening — so a genuine-looking peak cleared an afternoon-only
  reference that a full-day reference suppresses. Stopped captures are now
  spread across the retention window, the reference is the 85th percentile
  rather than the middle, and one spanning less than four hours is not trusted.
- Every finding judged against the reference says how many captures it rests on
  and how long they span.
- Requires Atrium 2.6.10.

## 1.9.7

- **Learns what the room is doing, so the room stops being diagnosed.** A
  bearing that is not turning has no cage frequency, yet captures taken with the
  motor stopped were reporting a "6203 FTF" peak at 18.3 Hz — ambient building
  vibration handed a bearing's name. Captures where the machine is detected as
  stopped now contribute a low-band ambient profile for that monitoring point,
  and anything found below running speed must stand clear of it before it can
  count toward severity. Where a point has no stopped captures yet the gate
  cannot be evaluated, and affected findings are reported as ambiguous rather
  than counted — an unanswerable question is not a pass.
- Requires Atrium 2.6.9. On an older platform the profile is simply unused.

## 1.9.6

- **The AI report is told what the engine's severity is made of.** The engine no
  longer derives severity from the ISO zone alone (Atrium 2.6.8), so the prompt
  no longer describes it as "the ISO 10816 velocity severity" — it now reads the
  new `severity_terms` block, which lists every term and what each contributed,
  including the ones that contributed nothing. Where the sensor's low-pass
  filter truncated the velocity band, the ISO term carries a caveat saying so,
  and the model is instructed to weigh the spectral evidence above the zone in
  that case.

## 1.9.5

- **Fixes 1.9.4 on the gateway.** The filter cutoff was read for every capture
  and always came back empty, so analysis kept reporting half the sample rate as
  usable bandwidth exactly as before. The lookup needed the sensor id and the
  query feeding it did not return one. A failed lookup is now logged rather than
  silently treated as "this sensor has no filter configured" — the two are not
  the same, and conflating them is what hid this.

## 1.9.4

- **Analysis now knows where the sensor's low-pass filter sits.** AssetPulse
  reads the sensor's reported filter setting and passes the real cutoff to the
  analysis, which previously assumed usable bandwidth ran to half the sample
  rate. On the default filter coefficient the true cutoff is a quarter of the
  sample rate — half what was assumed — so the spectrum between the two was
  filter roll-off being presented as signal.

  10816 velocity band is truncated and the zone reads healthier than the machine
  is. The assessment now says so instead of reporting the zone as if it were a
  compliant measurement.

  The cutoff is worked out from each capture's **measured** sample rate rather
  than the configured one, because a sensor keeps running its old settings until
  its next sync — which can be hours after you change them.

  **Needs platform 2.6.4.** On an older gateway the setting is read but ignored.

## 1.9.3

- **You can now clear a monitoring point's vibration baseline.** Each point
  learns a healthy reference from its first few captures and then freezes it,
  grading everything afterwards against that figure. Freezing is what makes a
  rising trend meaningful — and it is also why clearing needs to be possible.
  The reference is a vibration amplitude, so anything that changes what the
  sensor measures invalidates it without the machine having changed: a new
  full-scale range, a different output data rate, re-mounting the sensor, or
  simply having learned the reference while the machine was not running
  normally.

  Until now the only way out was deleting the monitoring point, which threw away
  its captures and alarm limits too. **Asset → Setup → Vibration Baselines**
  shows each point's state — established, still learning, or not started — with
  a Clear button per point and a Clear all for the sensor-settings case. The
  point relearns from its next captures.

  Clearing affects future captures; the asset keeps showing its last
  "vs. baseline" figure until the next one is analysed.

## 1.9.2

- **The per-capture fault list is gone.** It came from a heuristic detector
  whose confidences were not meaningful — on a healthy benchtop rig it reported
  nine simultaneous faults at 75–100%, identically at two different shaft
  speeds. AssetPulse already excluded it from the severity score and stripped it
  out of the AI report prompt; it is now gone from the app's data as well, and
  the app no longer writes it back to the platform.

  Nothing is lost. The asset's severity band, its ISO 10816 zone, the kinematic
  diagnoses and the AI assessment were always the real analysis, and they were
  being crowded out by a list of confident-looking findings that nothing in the
  product actually believed.

  sensor page keeps its own Detected Faults card, which AssetPulse cannot reach.

## 1.9.1

- **Adding a component to an existing asset duplicated the rest of the
  drivetrain.** Reported from the field: an assistant adding a fan to a
  configured machine ended up with a second copy of every component after it.
  A component was being recognised by its *position* in the chain, so inserting
  anything shifted everything downstream and none of it matched what was already
  there — so it was all added again.

  caller supplies one (read back from the asset's setup, which is the exact and
  preferred way), otherwise by its type and name, otherwise by type in order.
  Inserting or re-ordering is now safe.

  wrote the new order back, so a re-sent chain kept its old sequence. It now
  re-orders as sent. A component you leave out of the chain is still kept — it
  is moved to the end and reported back to the caller rather than being deleted.

  guidance that shapes the next one.** Two reads and one write:

  - **Read the exact prompt.** The verbatim `system` and `user` text AssetPulse

    the drivetrain and bearing context, the machine-off guidance, your own
    clauses, and the required output contract, in the order the model receives
    them. When a report says something you disagree with, this is how you find
    out what it was actually told. Defaults to the latest assessment; an older
    one can be inspected by id.

    content and enabled flag, plus which ones apply to a given asset, in the
    order they reach the model.
  - **Write a clause.** Create or update a clause and attach it to an asset in

    that clause — including for every other asset already using it, since the
    library is shared. Detaching and disabling are both supported, and they are

  nothing, with no error and nothing in the logs. Affected **Delete asset**

  occasionally did not. A call that does not fit is now refused by the gateway

  this version unlocks it on any gateway it is installed on — nothing to enter,
  nothing to activate, and existing licenses simply stop being consulted. Its
  AI-agent reads become visible too: an unlicensed app's API answers 402, so a
  gateway that had AssetPulse locked was not offering any of its tools to a

  photo of its nameplate — and turn that into a configured, monitored asset.

    used to exist only as dropdowns in the setup wizard, which is no help to
    something with no dropdowns.

  grants deliberately when issuing it; every call is recorded in the gateway's
  app audit log. Without that scope an assistant can still read everything above
  and tell you what it would create.

  returning no match where the plain "6205Z" form worked, because the trailing

  approved gateway. Choosing the proxy asks for its base URL, which API it
  presents (OpenAI Responses, OpenAI Chat Completions or Anthropic Messages), the

  nudging them, so an automation re-asserted after a reboot lands on the same
  configuration. Leaving a level empty clears it, so a critical-only alarm is
  just critical with warning blank. Omitting one of the notify or waveform flags

  fire on its own.

  the waveform window itself. Downloads the capture being viewed as a single
  `.zip`: the raw time-domain samples as CSV (`time_s, x_g, y_g, z_g`) plus a
  JSON sidecar with the asset, drivetrain, sensor, bearing and capture context
  needed to analyse it in another tool. Stepping through history with Older /
  Newer moves the download with it, so a past capture no longer has to be

## 1.4.0

- **Step through waveform history** — the View Waveform window now has

  is what makes two captures actually comparable.

## 1.3.0

**Requires gateway platform 2.4.0 or newer.** AssetPulse 1.3.0 will not install
on an older gateway — stay on 1.2.0 until the gateway is updated.

### Automations (inter-app bus)

AssetPulse can now take part in gateway automations, in both directions. It
publishes what it knows and exposes things it can do; you connect them to the
rest of the gateway on the **Automations** page. AssetPulse never talks to
another app directly — every crossing is a binding you create.

**Publishes (use as a "When"):**

- **Metric crossed a threshold** — where one metric on one monitoring point
  stands against its Warning / Critical thresholds. Match on `warning_breached`
  / `critical_breached` for "at this level or worse" — they stay true as a
  reading escalates, so an automation holds instead of releasing when the machine
  gets worse. `metric_state` gives one band exclusively when that's what you
  want. Tracked separately per monitoring point and metric.
- **Asset health changed** — an asset's severity band, running state, open
  alert count, and the latest AI assessment text and recommended action. Tracked
  per asset.

**Can do (use as a "Then"):**

- **Capture a vibration waveform** — request a raw capture from a monitoring
  point now. It runs through the severity engine like any other capture, so the
  asset's health is re-evaluated from it.
- **Acknowledge threshold alerts** — clear an asset's open alerts, optionally
  only Warning or only Critical.
- **Send asset health email** — send an asset's configured email now, using its
  own recipients, templates and latest AI report. Recorded in the asset's
  notification history.

State is republished periodically, so an automation reconciles on its own after
a gateway restart or a dropped message rather than staying stuck.

### Also

- **Settings → Automations** — a new card listing everything AssetPulse offers
  the bus, plus each asset's currently published health.
- Deleting an asset or monitoring point, or switching a threshold off, now
  clears its automation state instead of leaving an automation latched on
  something that no longer exists.

## 1.2.0

- **MQTT publishing** — publish Summary, Waveform, AI Report and Alert streams
  to the gateway's shared MQTT broker, with per-stream topic templates using the
  `::Token::` convention. Configure under **Settings → MQTT**. Requires the
  operator to grant AssetPulse in the gateway's MQTT Client settings.
- **AI settings** — added a connection **Test** button and **Clear key**.

## 1.1.1

- Overview refreshes in place instead of reloading the view.

## 1.1.0

- Compatibility with the sandboxed app host and scoped per-app tokens.

AssetPulse

Predictive maintenance for rotating equipment: set up assets, monitor vibration, and get plain-language health insights.

What it does

  • Organize your plant into assets (motors, pumps, fans, gearboxes) and pair

each with a vibration sensor.

  • Continuously monitors vibration and surfaces developing faults before they

cause unplanned downtime.

  • Turns the analysis into plain-language health insights so you don't need a

vibration analyst to act on the data.

  • Waveform history and export — step through past captures with ‹ Older /

Newer › to compare them directly, and download any capture as a .zip containing the raw time-domain samples as CSV plus a JSON sidecar with the asset, drivetrain, sensor and bearing context needed to analyse it elsewhere.

  • Takes part in gateway automations — publishes asset health and threshold

crossings that other apps can react to, and offers actions they can trigger: capture a waveform, acknowledge alerts, send a health email, or set an alarm threshold.

  • Answers questions from an AI assistant connected to the gateway — the

asset roster, how each machine is built, and what its alarm limits are.

  • Optionally publishes to MQTT — stream summary telemetry, waveform captures,

AI reports, and alerts to your own broker on operator-defined topics.

Requirements

  • Atrium platform 2.4.0 or newer.
  • Gateway model EG5120 (the vibration analysis is CPU-intensive and is not

supported on the EG5100).

  • One or more NCD vibration sensors paired with the gateway.

Two features need a newer platform and are simply not offered on an older one — AssetPulse installs and runs either way:

  • AI-agent access (the reads below) needs platform 2.6.0.
  • Routing AI reports through an AI gateway needs a platform that supports it.

Licensing

AssetPulse is a licensed app. You can install it from the App Center at any time, but it stays locked until a signed license bound to your gateway is entered on the app's License screen. Contact NCD to obtain a license.

Configuration

  • AI & Reports (optional) — generate plain-language reports from an AI

provider. Start by choosing the Connection: Direct to AI provider, or Through an AI proxy (AI gateway) for sites whose policy is that all AI traffic goes through an approved gateway. A proxy asks for its base URL, which API it presents (OpenAI Responses, OpenAI Chat Completions, or Anthropic Messages), the model route your proxy administrator gave you, and the proxy's own token — not the model vendor's, since the proxy holds that credential. Any extra headers live under Advanced. Test validates the configuration before you save.

Whichever connection you choose, the key is encrypted on the gateway and never displayed again, outbound calls follow the gateway's proxy settings, and what is sent is structured evidence only — never raw waveforms.

  • Notifications (optional) — email maintenance staff on severity increases;

requires SMTP configured on the gateway.

  • MQTT (optional) — enable MQTT publishing and set a topic template per data

stream (Summary, Waveform, AI Reports, Alerts). Topics support ::Token:: replacement (asset name, gateway id, sensor id, etc.); leave a topic blank to disable that stream. The gateway's broker connection is configured in the platform's Settings → MQTT Client, where the operator must also grant AssetPulse permission to publish.

  • Automations — Settings → Automations lists everything AssetPulse

offers the gateway bus, plus each asset's currently published health. You wire those to other apps on the platform's Automations page.

  • AI-agent access (optional, platform 2.6.0+) — AssetPulse's reads are

reachable only by an API token or connected app you grant the App data (apps:data) scope. Nothing is exposed until you grant it.

Permissions

  • data:read — reads telemetry from the platform database (read-only).
  • telemetry:subscribe — receives live sensor frames for alert evaluation.
  • radio:fft — requests and analyzes raw vibration waveforms.
  • notify:email — sends fault/alert emails via the gateway mailer.
  • net:external — reaches the configured AI provider or AI gateway for reports.
  • secrets — stores the AI provider or proxy key encrypted at rest.
  • mqtt:client — publishes on the gateway's shared MQTT client (the operator

must also grant AssetPulse in Settings → MQTT Client).

  • events:publish — announces asset health and threshold state on the gateway's

inter-app bus.

  • actions:provide — lets an automation trigger a waveform capture, an alert

acknowledgement, a health email, or a threshold change.

  • mcp:tools — opts AssetPulse into AI-agent access, so the reads listed above

can be called by an assistant you have granted the App data scope.

versions.readme_html:
MultiViz

Sends vibration data from NCD wireless sensors to Viking Analytics MultiViz, the self-learning machine-health monitoring platform. Enter the broker details from MultiViz's Setup Integration wizard, link the sensors you want monitored, and the app publishes their processed data and vibration waveforms to MultiViz, which builds its asset tree from them.

Requires Atrium 2.8.0 or later (the app's own MQTT connection to the MultiViz broker). Status: 0.1.2.

What it does

The app opens its own dedicated MQTT connection to the broker MultiViz's integration wizard provisions per customer, and publishes every frame from a linked sensor — processed (sensor_data.mode 0/2/3) and waveform (mode 1, sensor_data.data.{x,y,z}) — exactly as Atrium decoded it (the NCD structure: nodeId, firmware, battery, sensor_data, sensor_name, addr, received, rssi, …; the platform strips original before apps see the frame) on <topic_root>/<device_id>. A partial waveform (packets lost: fewer samples, fft_confidence < 100%, and the decoder sets sensor_data.error to "Time Series Data Stream Timeout - incomplete data received") is still published; its Historical row says how much arrived.

Type 127 (Vibration, Ultrasound and Temperature): the overall frame adds ultrasonic_rms_dBuV, ultrasonic_peak_to_peak_dBuV and crest_factor and is published as-is, as is its accelerometer waveform (sensor_data.source_type: "accelerometer", data.{x,y,z}). Its ultrasound waveform (source_type: "ultrasound", data a single array of dBuV samples, fsr: "120dbuV") is not published — MultiViz takes accelerometer waveforms only — and is noted in Historical as "Ultrasound waveform — not sent" (it doesn't count as a received waveform either).

Types 80 / 81 (One / Two Channel Vibration Plus — the pre-Gen4 line, supported for its C1D2 certification): overall frames are published as-is. Their waveform has no mode and arrives as numbered points (sensor_data.data = {"1": {x, y, z}, "2": …}); the app reshapes it to the Gen4 form (data: {x: [...], y: [...], z: [...]}, only the axes en_axis enabled) before publishing and leaves every other key as decoded (no mode, no total_samples — the decoder doesn't send them). They don't send waveforms on their own and take only the Regular request, with their own bytes: 80 F4 4F 00 00 54 13; 81 F4 4F 00 00 50 13 p with p 01 / 02 / 03 = both (sent with fft._transmit, since sendRequestNow would send FF). They can't be configured through Atrium: no Configure button, and linking one shows a V3-specific popup instead (no auto waveform — use On-request Waveform Data; configure mode, destination address, payload length, … with Node-RED; NCD technical support for guidance).

Sensor error frames are not published — MultiViz expects data frames only, for now. frameError() in backend/vibration.js recognizes NCD's shapes: sensor_data = { error, probe } with no mode (a type 111 probe that failed to sample), or no sensor_data at all with top-level data = { probe_1_error, probe_2_error } (type 111, both probes) or data = { error } (older types). Each skipped frame is recorded in the sensor's Historical popup as "Sensor error — not sent" with the sensor's message, and no waveform request is sent on it. MultiViz builds its own asset tree from the published data on its side — there is no site/area/machine/... mapping in this app, unlike an earlier version of it.

It also sends an on-request waveform data request — Regular, Custom (ODR + duration in the command) or Smart (waveform only if the motor runs, else MOFF) — after every processed transmission from a sensor, while the operator has it saved and enabled. The getting-started hardware settings (smart threshold/skip count, data transmission interval, auto waveform interval and destination address) are set from the Sensor Basic Hardware Settings popup; everything else stays on the sensor's own Sensor Configuration tab.

Waveforms arrive on the same sensor_data event as processed frames (the platform's own FFT module reads them there too), so both go out through one publisher. A 2-channel (type 111) sensor is linked as one sensor: Atrium decodes both probes into one processed frame (s1_/x1_/y1_/z1_/rpm_1 and the same with 2, no probe field), published whole; its waveforms carry sensor_data.probe. The On-request Waveform Data popup still picks a probe, because the request command has a probe byte.

On-request waveform data: a sleeping sensor only listens for ~1-2 s after it sends processed data, so Save + Enable only record the request; the sensor_data handler sends it on every processed frame (mode 2 Processed + Raw on demand, or 3 Smart — mode 0 never listens and the UI says so) until it's disabled. A duplicate frame within 3 s doesn't send twice. Commands (backend/vibration.js, probe byte 01 / 02 / FF = both):

  • Regular F4 4F 00 00 50 13 p — via the documented fft.sendRequestNow

(one both command, not two requests).

  • Custom F4 4F 00 00 00 54 p ODR duration (ODR 07–0D, duration 1–100 × 50 ms)
  • Smart F4 4F 00 00 65 50 p (probe 1 or 2 only)

Custom and Smart go through fft._transmit — see Known gaps. Per-probe request/receive times (waveform_probe_status) are shown per probe in the popup; the Overview row's icon combines the probes the request covers (received = every covered probe's waveform arrived after the latest request).

Data model

  • app_config — key/value app settings.
  • broker_settings — single row: the MultiViz broker connection (host, port,

TLS, username, password — encrypted via ctx.secrets, topic root, client ID, enabled).

  • linked_devices — one row per sensor that publishes to MultiViz. probe

is always '' now; an earlier version linked a 2-channel sensor per probe ('1'/'2'), and migration 005 merged those into one row.

  • waveform_settings — one row per device_id: the saved on-request

request (type/probe/ODR/duration, saved_at) and whether it's enabled (request_armed, kept from the earlier one-shot design; migration 004 disarmed old rows so an upgrade never starts continuous requests on its own).

  • publish_log — the last 50 events per device behind the Historical popup:

overall / waveform (published; detail notes an incomplete waveform), error (a sensor error frame that was skipped; detail holds the sensor's message — migration 006) and ultrasound (a type 127 ultrasound waveform that was skipped).

  • waveform_probe_status — per (device_id, probe): last request sent,

last waveform received. Still has unused dest_addr/auto_/_option_key columns from an earlier version of this app that configured destination address and Auto Waveform Data itself (removed in favor of linking to the sensor's own settings page) — left in place rather than dropped, since 001-init.sql already shipped.

Platform touchpoints (matches capabilities)

  • data:read — reads atrium.devices, atrium.sensor_meta,

atrium.gateway_config.

  • telemetry:subscribe — sensor_data: publish trigger, request trigger,

and waveform-received tracking.

  • secrets — encrypts the broker password at rest; decrypted ingest-side to

open the connection.

  • mqtt:connect — ctx.services.mqttConnections, this app's own broker

connection (mqttConnections.open("multiviz", …)), ingest-side only.

  • sensor:config — ctx.services.sensorConfig: the Sensor Basic Hardware

Settings popup reads the getting-started settings (smart threshold(s), skip count, sampling_interval / auto_raw_interval / auto_raw_destination_address, shown as Data Transmission Interval, Auto Waveform Transmission Interval and Auto Waveform Destination Address — only keys getOptions() lists for the sensor) with get() (reported/desired + sync_status) and saves them with setDesired() (whitelisted keys, range-checked first; delivered at the sensor's next check-in). Also reads atrium.gateway_config.modem_mac for "Use this Atrium".

  • radio:fft — ctx.services.fft.sendRequestNow (Regular) and

fft._transmit (Custom/Smart, undocumented — see Known gaps); also registers a capture claimer for linked sensors.

Configuration

Set up via the app's own UI:

  1. Overview — broker connection status with a Configure popup

(broker URL/port/credentials/topic root from MultiViz's Setup Integration wizard, Test connection, Connect/Disconnect, Save), linked/not-linked counts, and the Linked Sensors table (newest link first; a sensor just linked from Manage Sensors is highlighted for 5 s, tagged "Newly linked"): a Report switch per link that pauses MQTT publishing without unlinking (takes effect immediately — the UI pokes the ingest daemon's links/reload route), last seen / last MQTT report, Last Seen on Atrium, Last Report MultiViz, and per-row Configure (gear icon: Sensor Basic Hardware Settings popup, with Reset to current values; the full settings stay on Atrium's Sensor Configuration tab), Historical, Details, On-request Waveform Data (icon shows the request status) and Remove (asks for confirmation).

  1. Manage Sensors — every vibration sensor on the gateway with its

Linked / Linked · Paused / Not linked state, and the form to link one (a 2-channel sensor is linked whole). A new link starts with its Report switch OFF, and a popup suggests configuring the sensor first (for a V3 type 80/81, a popup explaining what's different about it). Linked sensors drop out of the picker; removing a link puts them back.

  1. On-request Waveform Data popup (per sensor, from the Overview) —

choose Regular/Custom (Regular only for 80/81) and the probe (Smart is implemented but hidden in the UI for now, unless a Smart request is already saved), Save, then Enable/Disable. It notes that a Gen4 sensor already sending waveforms automatically (Auto Waveform Transmission Interval) doesn't need it. Destination address and auto waveform transmission are set from the Configure popup (Gen4) or Node-RED (80/81).

Tooltips render through a portal into document.body (components/Tooltip.jsx): a CSS-only ::after tooltip gets clipped by the scrolling tables and the modal body.

Limitations

  • Requesting a waveform after every transmission costs sensor battery and

airtime; the On-request Waveform Data popup says so. A Gen4 sensor already sending waveforms on its own (Auto Waveform Transmission Interval) doesn't need it.

  • Sensor error frames and type 127 ultrasound waveforms are not sent to

MultiViz; each is noted in the sensor's Historical popup.

  • Types 80 / 81 can't be configured from Atrium; use Node-RED, or contact NCD

technical support.

  • Custom and Smart waveform requests rely on a platform internal and are

disabled automatically if a platform update removes it; Regular requests are unaffected.

versions.readme_html:
OEE

Standalone Overall Equipment Effectiveness tracking. Define your machines and shifts, then drive Availability, Performance, and Quality from sensors or manual entry — no other app required.

What it does

  • Organize your plant into machines, group them into views (lines,

cells, areas), and see a live OEE score for each machine, view, and the whole plant.

  • Each machine has three independently configurable slots — Availability,

Performance, and Quality — and each slot can be driven by a sensor (run-state signal, uptime counter, or parts counter) or by manual entry.

  • Define shifts with start/end times, weekdays, and a scheduled length; OEE is

measured against elapsed production time so far in the shift.

  • Downtime reason codes with auto-detected stops: the app surfaces stops it

measured from the Availability sensor and lets an operator assign a reason to each, then charts the top loss reasons as a Pareto.

  • Reject reason codes: assign reasons to sensor-counted rejects (the sensor

count stays authoritative) or log rejects by hand, with an "unclassified" bucket and a reject Pareto.

  • Per-machine OEE target drives consistent green/amber/red coloring across

every score in the app.

  • Set the machine's ideal rate in parts/min (stored as an ideal cycle time);

Performance is measured against it.

Requirements

  • Atrium platform 2.3.0 or newer.
  • Runs on both EG5120 and EG5100.
  • No other app required. OEE manages its own machine and shift configuration and

reads sensor telemetry directly.

versions.readme_html:
ProXR Control

Build custom control panels for NCD ProXR relay controllers reached over the gateway's DigiMesh radio.

What it does

An operator registers each ProXR board once (name, 64-bit DigiMesh address, relay count, analog input options), then assembles control panels from cards: command buttons, relay indicators, relay grids, analog input readouts and trend charts, and controller status. Cards can drive any command in the ProXR set — individual relays, whole banks, relay groups, patterns, on-board timers and flashers — and the app polls each board so the panels show the controller's actual reported state rather than what was last commanded.

Panels are laid out on a grid. A card is dragged to any cell, including an empty one on a row below, or nudged and resized a cell at a time with the arrows on the card; gaps are kept exactly where the operator leaves them rather than being closed up. The server validates every layout it is sent, so cards cannot overlap or hang off the panel.

Beyond the panels it ships:

  • Controller detail — per-relay toggles with friendly names, bank actions,

timed "on for N seconds" commands (the controller switches the relay back off by itself, so a lost gateway can't leave a load energized), analog input scaling into engineering units, and the board's own feature map read from its device identification bytes.

  • Sequences — ordered command lists with delays between steps (startup,

shutdown, test runs), runnable from a panel button.

  • Schedules — a command or a sequence at a time of day. Day of week, hour,

minute and second are each optional: an unset field that is coarser than the finest one set means "every", so a schedule with only the minute set runs once an hour, and one with only the hour set runs once a day. Finer unset fields are zero, so "hour = 6" is 06:00:00 rather than 3 600 firings. The page shows the rule in plain English and the next three firings before anything is saved, and "Run now" proves a schedule without waiting for its time. Times are evaluated in the gateway's display_timezone, so a schedule set for 06:00 stays at 06:00 across daylight-saving changes.

  • Command console — pick any command, see the exact API frame that will be

transmitted, send it, and read the raw reply decoded.

  • Activity — every operator-initiated command with the bytes exchanged, who

sent it and whether the controller answered.

  • Automations — controller state is published on the gateway's inter-app bus,

and four commands are exposed for an operator to trigger from anything else the gateway publishes. See Inter-app bus below.

It consumes no sensor telemetry: ProXR boards are not sensors, so nothing in atrium.readings is involved. The only platform hardware surface it uses is the DigiMesh peer the operator authorized for each board.

Data model

All in the app's own database (/overlay/apps/proxr-control/app.db).

| Table | Contents | Growth | |---|---|---| | app_config | Key/value app settings (retention windows, install timestamp). | Fixed. | | controllers | One row per ProXR board: name, DigiMesh address (unique), relay count, analog input settings, poll and sample intervals, enabled flag, cached device identification. | One row per board. | | relay_labels | Friendly name per relay, so cards inherit it. | ≤ relay count per board. | | adc_inputs | Label, unit, scale, offset, decimals and display range per analog input. | ≤ 8 per board. | | dashboards | User-built control panels. | A handful. | | widgets | One row per card: kind, title, controller override, action, parameters and options as JSON, and its grid cell and size (grid_x, grid_y, grid_w, grid_h). span/sort_order are kept in step so a panel built before the grid still reads correctly. | Tens per panel. | | scenes | Named command sequences (steps stored as JSON). | A handful. | | schedules | Name, target (command + parameters, or a sequence), the optional day/hour/minute/second fields, enabled flag, and the outcome of the last run. | A handful. | | controller_state | Last known relay banks, analog values, online flag and last error per controller. Written by the daemon on change only; this is how the API service (a separate process) sees live state. | One row per board. | | adc_samples | Sampled analog inputs for trend charts, one row per channel per sample. | See retention below. | | command_log | Operator-initiated commands: frame sent, frame received, outcome, duration, username. Polling traffic is deliberately not logged. | See retention below. |

Retention. adc_samples and command_log are the only tables that grow continuously, and both are pruned by a background worker in the daemon every 30 minutes using chunked deletes (5 000 rows per statement, capped per pass) so the write lock is never held long. Windows are configurable in the app's Settings page (app_config.adc_retention_hours, default 7 days; app_config.log_retention_hours, default 14 days). Worst case at the defaults — one board, 8 inputs, the fastest allowed 10 s sample interval — is roughly 480 k rows, a few tens of MB. At the default 60 s interval it is ~80 k rows.

Sampling is throttled independently of polling (adc_log_interval_ms, minimum 10 s), so a 2 s poll interval for responsive panels does not multiply stored rows.

Platform touchpoints (matches capabilities)

  • data:read — reads atrium.gateway_config (gateway model) and

atrium.digimesh_peers (to show whether a controller's radio is registered and enabled). Nothing in atrium.* is ever written.

  • digimesh:transmit — ctx.services.digimesh.transmit(address, bytes) to send

ProXR frames. Every call is audited by the platform.

  • digimesh:subscribe — ctx.services.digimesh.subscribe(address, handler) to

receive each board's replies. One subscription per enabled controller.

  • events:publish — ctx.bus.publish on the ingest side to announce controller,

relay and analog state; ctx.bus.retained on the API side to read it back for the Settings page.

  • actions:provide — the four handlers exported from backend/ingest/index.js,

so an operator can put a ProXR command on the "Then" side of a binding.

ctx.audit is used for console commands, sequence runs, every schedule firing and every command an automation triggers — unattended commands are exactly what an audit trail is for. No telemetry:subscribe, no email, no external network access, and no events:subscribe: this app does not watch the bus, because bindings need no code in it and keep the operator in control.

minPlatformVersion is 2.4.0, the release that added the bus. Without the floor an older gateway would install the app happily and then leave ctx.bus undefined — a runtime failure instead of an install-time one. The DigiMesh capabilities need 2.3.5, so 2.4.0 covers both.

Process split

Everything that touches the radio lives in backend/ingest — the daemon owns the radio, and ProXR boards are speak-when-spoken-to, so each controller has a serialized command queue with exactly one exchange in flight. The API plugin (backend/api) owns configuration, cards, sequences and history and never transmits. The frontend calls /api/apps/proxr-control/ for configuration and /api/apps/proxr-control/ingest/ for anything on the wire.

Schedules are evaluated in the daemon, once a second, because that is the process that can transmit. Every second between the previous tick and now is checked, so a busy event loop cannot silently drop a firing, and a schedule that already ran in a given second will not run again — the guard is the persisted timestamp, so it survives a restart inside that same second. A tick more than a minute behind (service restart) is not replayed.

Polling costs one exchange for relays plus one for analog inputs. Boards with more than 8 relays use the single 32-bank read; if that command goes unanswered three times (some firmware revisions don't implement it) the daemon falls back permanently to one read per populated bank and logs the switch.

backend/lib/proxr.js is the single source of truth for the protocol: frame building, checksums, the action catalog with its parameter ranges, the incremental frame parser, and response decoding. The frontend renders its command and card forms from catalogs served out of that file (GET /actions, GET /widget-kinds), so the two sides cannot drift.

Inter-app bus

The app has no idea what is on the other end of a binding, and contains no other app's id: it publishes its state, it exposes commands, and the operator wires the two on the gateway's Automations page. That click is the authorization — this app holds digimesh:transmit, and letting another app ask it to fire a relay would hand that app radio authority it never declared.

Published state (provides.events)

Level-triggered current state, keyed per thing, republished on every evaluation. Publishing the same value twice dispatches nothing; the opposite value dispatches the exit edge, so a binding self-heals after a dropped message or a restart instead of latching on.

| Topic | Keyed per | Published when | |---|---|---| | controller.status | controller | Every poll; also the moment a board's radio turns out not to be authorized, which is the only state an un-subscribable board ever has. | | relay.state | controller + relay number | Every poll. A relay that has never been read is not published — an automation must not act on a value the app invented. | | analog.input | controller + input channel | On the board's adc_log_interval_ms, scaled and labelled exactly as the panel cards show it, so a threshold means what it means on screen. |

Every payload declares its fields, with enum: where the values are fixed, since that is what populates the operator's condition builder. controller.status carries both status (online/offline) and online (bool) deliberately: the enum gives a dropdown, the bool reads better interpolated into an email.

What is deliberately not published: the radio round-trip time. It is on the controller page and in /ingest/state, but it is a gauge, not state — it changes on nearly every poll, so a level-triggered event carrying it announces a "change" every few seconds forever. On a test gateway it was 56% of everything this app put on the bus. The general rule for anything added here: if a field moves on its own without the thing it describes having changed, it does not belong in the payload.

Rate limit. The platform allows 120 publishes per minute per topic, and a 32-relay board polled every 5 s would want 384 on relay.state alone. backend/lib/bus.js handles this: a key publishes the instant its state changes, every key is re-asserted on a sweep whose cadence is derived from the number of keys (60 re-assertions a minute, so a bigger installation heartbeats more slowly), and a per-topic budget below the platform's limit spends on changes before re-assertions. A refused or throttled publish is retried on the next evaluation rather than swallowed.

Re-assertion is a safety net, not a heartbeat — it exists to repair a dropped message or a restarted broker. The floor is 5 minutes, because on a small install the floor is the rate, and a sweep re-asserting two keys every 30 s is most of what ends up in the event log. A key a poll published within half its topic's own interval is skipped, so the sweep and a poll cannot publish the same key twice in a tick.

Exposed commands (provides.actions)

Ingest-side only, because every one of them touches the radio. All absolute and idempotent — relay.set with a state, never relay.toggle, because a binding is re-asserted after a gateway restart and a relative command would invert the load.

| Action | Parameters | |---|---| | relay.set | controller, relay, on/off, and an optional auto-off in seconds. The auto-off is handed to the controller's own duration timer, so the load is released even if this gateway stops answering; the timer index is derived from the relay number, so re-asserting the same relay reuses it instead of leaving two timers racing. | | bank.set | controller, bank (0 = every bank), on/off. | | flasher.set | controller, flasher 1-16, on/off. | | sequence.run | a sequence built on the Sequences page. |

Parameters come from a human filling in a form, so every handler validates them and throws a message the operator can act on (controller 4 is not configured on this gateway, not Cannot read properties of undefined). The controller and sequence fields are dropdowns rather than boxes to type an id into, fed by GET /bus/options/controllers and GET /bus/options/sequences — the paths named by options_from in the manifest.

Commands triggered this way are written to the command log with source automation, or automation_test when the operator pressed Run now, so the Activity page does not make a test look like a real firing. Each one is also audited with the binding's name.

GET /bus (API side) returns the declared catalog plus the retained state the daemon last published, which is what the Settings page's Automations panel shows; GET /ingest/bus returns the publisher's counters, which only the daemon has.

Configuration

The customer must do two things before the app can talk to a board:

  1. Register the radio under Settings → Devices → DigiMesh Peers on the

gateway, using the radio module's 64-bit MAC. Apps cannot register their own peers — that registration is the authorization model. Until it exists, the controller shows "not authorized" with the address to add, and the daemon retries the subscription every 15 s so it starts working without a restart.

  1. Set the radio to transparent mode (AP=0) and point its destination

(DH/DL) at this gateway or broadcast. In API mode the ProXR board receives framed bytes it cannot parse and never answers, while transmit still reports delivery — the radio did receive it.

Then add the controller in the app (name, address, relay count) and press "Read now". Wiring notes are repeated in the app's Settings page so the operator does not need this file.

Nothing else is required: no SMTP, no API keys, no sensor assignment.

Safety notes surfaced in the UI

  • Relay state is the controller's memory state, which is what ProXR reports.

A damaged relay, an unpowered expansion board or severe EMI can make the physical relay disagree with it.

  • Expansion boards must be powered simultaneously with the main controller,

never after it.

  • Buttons that switch real loads can be marked "ask for confirmation", and

momentary buttons send the inverse command on release. For anything where a lost link must not leave a load on, use a timed command instead — the controller enforces the timeout itself.

Testing done

  • Off-gateway unit checks: node tools/proxr-selftest.js in the parent

development repo checks every command frame this app can build against the byte-for-byte tables in the NCD ProXR quick start guide (183 checks: frames, checksums, response decoding including the device identification worked example, radio-fragmented frame reassembly and resync, relay/bank numbering, address normalization, card validation, panel geometry including deliberate gaps and refused overlaps, and schedule matching — partial fields, day sets, predicted firings, and both daylight-saving transitions). It also documents the three places where the guide's printed values are internally inconsistent (the "Activate All Timers" mask, the timer query length byte, and the write-scratchpad checksums) — in each case the frame this app sends is the one the guide's own arithmetic supports. The bus checks additionally assert that the manifest and the code describe the same events and actions in both directions — no undeclared payload field, no handler without a declaration, no relative action, and no options_from pointing at a path the API does not serve.

  • Off-gateway integration: node tools/proxr-integration.js runs the real

API plugin and daemon against a real SQLite database (migrations applied in order) and a simulated radio that answers ProXR frames, covering controller and panel creation, layout persistence and the backfill of pre-grid panels, rejection of illegal layouts, subscription and polling, a schedule firing on its second exactly once, run-now, and a schedule on an unauthorized radio recording the failure. The bus half runs against a broker that validates every publish against app.json and rate limits per topic the way the platform does: state published under stable per-thing keys, an unchanged relay not republished, each action driving the simulated board, each rejecting bad operator input with an actionable message, and the API service reading the daemon's retained state back. node tools/proxr-dev-server.js serves the same stack on localhost:3001 for npm start against a simulated board, and stands in for the platform's /api/bus/catalog and /api/bus/events plus a POST /api/bus/run/<action> that does what a binding's Run now does.

  • Frontend: production CRA build clean (no warnings), MemoryRouter seeded

from window.location, scoped-token handshake from the template unchanged, all polling at the platform's 5 s convention or slower and cleaned up on unmount. Absolute times render in the gateway's display_timezone and "x minutes ago" is measured against the gateway's clock (/api/system/time), so a skewed browser clock doesn't make a live board look stale.

  • Gateway model(s): _pending — needs a 2.4.0+ gateway with a registered ProXR

peer._

  • Platform version: _pending._
  • Checklist (docs/11-checklist.md): manifest, backend, database, frontend and

inter-app bus sections verified by inspection and by the two suites above. The "On-gateway verification" section is outstanding and needs hardware, and with it the two bus items that can only be proved on a gateway: that GET /api/bus/catalog lists all three events and all four actions with invocable true, and that publishing a matching state twice dispatches a binding only once.

Commercial intent

To be decided with NCD. The app is complete and self-contained either way.

Changelog

  • 0.2.1 — stop controller.status publishing on a timer. The payload carried the

radio round-trip time, which changes on nearly every poll, so an idle board announced a state change every 5 s; on a test gateway 477 events in 52 minutes carried 4 real changes. The round-trip time is no longer published (it stays on the controller page), and the re-assertion floor moves from 30 s to 5 minutes.

  • 0.2.0 — inter-app bus: controller, relay and analog state published as

level-triggered events, and relay.set, bank.set, flasher.set and sequence.run exposed for an operator to wire to anything else the gateway publishes. Raises minPlatformVersion to 2.4.0.

  • 0.1.0 — initial release: controllers, control panel builder with 9 card types on

a free-form grid, the full ProXR command catalog, sequences, schedules, command console, activity log, analog input scaling and trends, configurable retention.

# Changelog

## 1.0.1

**Fixed — schedules could stop firing until the ingest service restarted.**

A schedule's in-flight guard could be stranded on a stale object. While a
scheduled command was in flight, the 15-second controller/schedule reload
rebuilt each schedule entry as a new object and copied the `running` flag
forward; the command's completion handler then cleared the flag on the old
object that had already been replaced. The schedule was skipped from then on,
and every later reload copied the stuck flag forward again — only restarting
`atrium-ingest` cleared it.

Schedule entries are now updated in place, so the in-flight guard is always set
and cleared on the same object the scheduler reads.

Any schedule whose command overlapped a reload could be affected; longer-running
sequences were the most exposed. Schedules an exact multiple of 15 seconds apart
shared the same timer phase and so could stick within a short span of each other.

## 1.0.0

Initial release.

Machine run time for plant managers and shop foremen: what is running right now, and how much each machine has run.

What it does

running, stopped or has lost its signal, live as the sensor reports it.

  • Run time and cycles for each machine per shift, day, week, month, quarter,

  • Setup wizard that configures the run-detection sensor for you:
  • For vibration sensors, it measures a threshold from the machine's own raw

accelerometer data, with the machine off and then running.

  • For AC current sensors (type 33), it finds the current threshold by testing

it with the machine running and stopped, then suggests one between the two.

  • Service hours: an hours-since-service odometer with an estimated due date,

a Service view listing what is due, and a service log.

  • Alerts: an email and a red tile when a machine has been stopped too long,

and an email and a badge when service is due.

  • Works with other apps and AI assistants: publishes machine state, running

and alert events on the gateway's app bus, offers actions other apps can trigger, and lets an AI assistant connected to the gateway read the floor and run-time history.

This is deliberately not OEE: it measures how long machines run, not availability, performance and quality.

Supported sensors

Type 2 (two-channel contact), 33 (AC current detect), 108 (machine uptime monitor), 119 (machine runtime hour meter), and 123, 132 and 133 (production counters).

Requirements

  • Learning a type 33's current threshold needs platform 2.8.0. On an older

platform the wizard says so, and the threshold can be set by hand under Advanced.

  • One or more of the supported sensors paired with the gateway.

Configuration

Add each machine and bind it to one input of a sensor, then run the setup wizard. Settings covers tile options, shifts, the production day, groups, and how long before a silent sensor is reported as lost.

Type 119 input filter fixed too (Travis, 2026-10-15): debounce 1000 ms, `interrupt_timeout` 0 (firmware `Wireless_motor_uptime_monitor`, which also builds the 108 and 123: debounce restarts on every edge, so shorter flickers never become a report; `interrupt_timeout` is the counter-ignore window there as well). The wizard hides the speed choice for it. Where the choice remains (108, 123, 132, 133), `interrupt_timeout` is now labelled for what it does — the sensor's own cycle counter — not as a wait between reports.

Type 33 input filter is fixed, not a choice (Travis, 2026-10-15; confirmed in the firmware source, `NCD_Applications/applications/wireless_current_detect_oee_sensor`): debounce 1000 ms always (a plain per-edge filter; a CT's current is steady), and `interrupt_timeout` 0 — on this firmware it's `u16_ctr_ignore_timeout`, which only stops the sensor's own cycle counter counting more than once per window and holds back no transmissions, so it saves no battery.
